cards.answer: I’ve learned to question assumptions at every step. Before building logic, I check for hidden data fields that can change the outcome, like a quantity field that once shifted a headline figure by nearly half. cards.answer: I ran a controlled benchmark on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU comparing Ollama and vLLM. I isolated the model by using the same architecture in both to rule it out as a variable. cards.answer: I built a pipeline for archivists and researchers to explore email archives without opening messages, using pd.to_datetime with errors="coerce" to parse 20 years of date formats. A search across about 79,676 message rows for one sender returned 386 matching records without full-text indexing.

cards.answer: I built a semantic search engine that embeds LLaMA-generated summaries into FAISS HNSW indexes for fast approximate nearest-neighbor lookup. The search space is clean and normalized because it indexes summaries rather than raw text.

cards.answer: I chose the legislative pipeline's LLM through a formal evaluation of 3 models and 5 chunk sizes, tested in a 15-cell grid with service levels set before execution. Extraction across 11,673 bills took roughly 155 hours unattended. Output quality degraded past 2,000 tokens, so chunk size was decided separately from model choice. links.label: Procurement intelligence: The Unit Normalization Problem

cards.answer: I built a pack-size normalization system to uncover true per-unit pricing in procurement data, using the qsu field (quantity sold as), which is populated for 99.9% of rows (6,068,599 of 6,068,888). links.label: Research proposal pipeline: The HERDS Taxonomy

cards.answer: I built a 26-field taxonomy for the NSF HERDS classification system, using a curated and deduplicated keyword list with eight reassignments adjudicated per keyword. I embedded each proposal using SentenceTransformer and multiplied it against a pre-computed taxonomy-embedding matrix for all 26 fields in one operation. I blended semantic scores with keyword-overlap scores at 0.75 to 0.25 and set a MIN_SCORE_THRESHOLD of 0.12 to gate labels. This method outperformed either signal alone on the validation set.

cards.answer: I trained a separate Tree Ensemble model for each semester (Summer, Spring, and Fall) to capture term-specific dropout patterns. I applied SMOTE with k=5 nearest neighbors only to the 70% training partition, never the 30% held-out test set, to prevent leakage. cards.answer: I evaluated the Illinois Legislation Pipeline’s LLM inference stack, which extracts 15 structured fields from state bills for analysts and policy researchers. cards.answer: I designed a controlled vLLM evaluation using 50 identical 4,500 to 4,972 Mistral-token bills across three models: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 AWQ, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct AWQ, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct AWQ. Each model ran at its quality-best chunk size, avoiding forced uniformity, what I call the Olympic swimmer principle. I measured TTFT, ITL p50/p99, decode and prefill throughput with 10-second GPU sampling and no safety alarms. Setup used vLLM 0.6.6, AWQ-Marlin, --max-model-len 8192, prefix caching, and a 5-call warmup. I ran 3 repeats per cell, with cross-repeat variance under 0.5% throughput, 1.5% p99 latency, and 0.3pp quality.

cards.answer: I ran Experiment 3 to evaluate extraction quality beyond parse-OK by scoring 60 cells on Accuracy, Specificity and Completeness. I used Claude Opus 4.8 in two independent passes, high effort then max effort, and both agreed on 60 out of 60 with zero revisions. Parse-OK reliably ranks the three models in the same order as substantive scoring. But Experiment 3.5 showed parse-OK fails as a within-model proxy: smaller chunks scored higher in every informative pair. The mechanism is off-section drift. Larger chunks lead to confident answers about the wrong part of the bill. I found qwen_3000 returned parse_status=OK with all 11 fields set to None.

cards.answer: In March 2026 I evaluated LLM inference throughput using Ollama and later vLLM 0.6.6. Initially, Mistral 7B at chunk_size=500 was the top performer for the stack. cards.answer: I used the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) on the L4 GPU to assess infrastructure health, separate from output quality. The L4 showed effective saturation in single inference streams, with unmeasured concurrency headroom driving the vLLM migration. Testing Qwen 2.5 with 1,200 tokens, I found a p99 latency of 137s, versus 13 to 16s for healthy cells, throughput down 7 to 9x, and 32 of 165 chunks lost, reproduced three times. TTFT, ITL, KV cache utilization, and per-stream decode throughput were unmeasurable in Ollama and marked as known limitations.

cards.answer: I built a rubric with three dimensions scored 0 to 2: Accuracy, Specificity and Completeness. Accuracy measures from wrong (0) to faithful to this chunk (2). Specificity ranges from generic boilerplate (0) to naming the actual mechanism (2), and Completeness from a surface phrase (0) to a substantive point captured (2). The per-cell average is (Accuracy + Specificity + Completeness) / 3.

cards.answer: In the archival image project, I engineered the LLaVA Direct pipeline, which ran at about 9 images per minute in production, taking 22 hours to process 12,125 images. As the project scaled beyond the POC, this throughput became a constraint. I isolated the bottleneck using a controlled performance test on an NVIDIA L4 GPU, finding that GPU utilization stayed at 28 to 31% while p50 latency inflated 8.18x under concurrent requests, pointing to request serialization at the Ollama daemon.

cards.answer: I built a generative Markov chain model to simulate probable career journeys from any starting role across N moves. The simulate_career_path function walks transitions stochastically, while simulate_many_paths summarizes final-role distributions. links.label: UIC Student Enrollment Prediction: Data Preparation

cards.answer: I built four label variations for the UIC enrollment model to test different definitions of student continuation. Next Term labeled continuation as 1 if a student enrolled in the immediately following fall or spring term, with summer skips not penalized, graduation as 2, and dropout as 0. Next Year (Any Term) was more forgiving of gaps, checking for enrollment in any term within the following academic year. Next Fall Only isolated the strongest signal by looking only for fall term re-enrollment in the following year. Binary Success collapsed continuation and graduation into a single success label (1), with dropout as 0.

links.label: Quality Validation: Does parse-OK measure quality?

cards.answer: I built a quality review system using chunk-fidelity scoring, which evaluates whether a model correctly extracts a specific chunk of text rather than relying on whole-bill understanding. This method revealed that at Chunk 8, the model mistral_3000 produced a highly specific answer about a different section of the same bill. Under chunk-fidelity scoring, this was marked as Accuracy 1, but under whole-bill summarization, it would flip to Accuracy 2. Both passes flagged this single call as the turning point for the result.

cards.answer: I led Phase 1 quality validation across 20 chunks for three models: llama31_1200, qwen_500, and mistral_3000. The overall mean scores were 1.70 for llama31_1200, 1.58 for qwen_500, and 1.53 for mistral_3000. Parse-OK peaks were 92.5% for llama31_1200, 62.5% for qwen_500, and 72.0% for mistral_3000. cards.answer: I tested seven OCR and vision models against professional reference transcriptions to choose the best for historical book scanning. I measured character error, word accuracy, speed, and how often models invented or repeated text. The best engine had about 3% character error, while the traditional open-source OCR baseline had about 20%. Even the best model invented fluent Latin not on the page when faced with the oldest type, showing no model could be fully trusted alone.

cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM models using three quality signals. The first signal is a structural validity check, parse-OK rate, across all 15 fields, fast and scalable but not sufficient. The second is a blind rubric scoring of 60 cells across three models' best configurations to confirm parse-OK ranked them correctly. The third is within-model proxy validation, finding parse-OK failed to guide chunk-size optimization reliably.

cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM inference throughput across chunk sizes and found that Llama is the only model to clear 80% parse-OK at every size tested. All six Llama cells sit between 85.0% and 92.5%, while Mistral ranges from 56% to 72% and Qwen never reliably exceeds 73%. The gap between Llama's worst cell and any other model's best cell is still 12+ percentage points. Qwen shows a non-monotonic shape with a dip at 1,200 tokens. cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM inference throughput and found that at chunk_size=4,000, each bill split into a full 4,000-token chunk and a short 500 to 900-token tail chunk. These tails lacked enough content to populate all fields, so the extractor returned parse_partial. At chunk_size=5,000, the same bills became single chunks and Mistral's parse-OK recovered to exactly 72.0%, matching its chunk_size=3,000 result. I called this a corpus length artifact, not a model limitation.

cards.answer: I evaluated vLLM model performance by testing Llama, Mistral, and Qwen on three different lenses, finding Llama led by 13 to 27.5 percentage points depending on the framing. cards.answer: In experiment 3, I designed a scoring system using Claude Opus 4.8 to evaluate 60 cells (3 profiles, 20 chunks, and 3 dimensions) on a 0 to 2 rubric for Accuracy, Specificity, and Completeness. cards.answer: I evaluated how context-window size affects extraction fidelity in vLLM configurations. The 3,000-token Mistral config often pulled in adjacent bill sections and lost the chunk’s headline. The 1,200-token Llama config stayed on-chunk most reliably. The 500-token Qwen config was faithful but too compressed. On multi-section bills, Mistral’s score dropped while Llama held steady. This is a property of the configurations, not the models alone.

At Chunk 8, Mistral returned a highly specific but off-topic answer from the same bill, scoring Accuracy:1 under chunk-fidelity. cards.answer: I measured Mistral's root cause as KV cache head-of-line blocking, with preemption at concurrency eight or higher due to L4's 22.5 GB VRAM limits. I proposed three optimization paths: reducing chunk size to 2,000 tokens to ease cache pressure and improve quality, increasing vLLM swap space from 4 GB to 16+ GB, and adjusting chunking strategy to match real-world data like short bills.

cards.answer: I evaluated Qwen 7B’s failure modes and two paths. I read None-emission, where all 11 fields return None, as a prompt compliance issue, not a model capability one. Path 1 is to add explicit field-completion requirements, return 'not mentioned' rather than null, and two-shot examples, then rerun Exp 3.5 Pair 2 and measure whether None-emission drops below 5%. Path 2 is chunk_size=2,000 as the operating point, since it scored 1.93 quality versus 1.57 at chunk_size=3,000. Qwen’s ITL p99 of 118ms versus Llama’s 49ms is likely caused by its tokenizer; capping max_tokens at 768 may stabilize ITL.

cards.answer: I evaluated Qwen 14B's output constraints and found that at 5,000 input tokens, the model lacked headroom to complete 11-field JSON responses, with 54% partial parses and 1.2 missing fields on average. Path 1: increase max_tokens to 2,048, which gives about 2x output headroom at roughly 40 to 60% slower per call; Path 2: reduce chunk_size to 2,000, which leaves about 3,000 tokens of output headroom. The throughput ceiling is about 0.15 to 0.20 chunks per second, making the 14B model 2 to 3x slower than Llama unless hardware improves.

cards.answer: During the extended sweep, I spotted silent failures where launches exited with code 0 but produced incomplete results. Files of 761 bytes instead of 4 to 5 KB, and wall times of 3 seconds instead of 5 minutes. The issue was a tokenizer cache miss caused by an SSL handshake failure to an external host. I identified it by checking file sizes, wall times, and chunks_written counts rather than relying on exit codes. cards.answer: I designed the vLLM evaluation to make a production decision, not to run a benchmark, because choosing the wrong model could become a liability as more states are added. cards.answer: The article shows the Illinois corpus has a median bill length of 1,051 tokens, 75% under 3,500 tokens, and a tail to 1 million tokens. Mistral's parse-OK dropped from 72% to 59.8% at chunk size 4,000 because sample bills split into a 500 to 900 token tail chunk and recovered to 72.0% at 5,000. The SLO was about 75,000 bills per week at 50-state scale in an 18-hour window and the gap on one L4 was 3.16x steady state and 6.57x peak burst. Three L4s in parallel or one A100-class GPU would close the steady-state gap. The four practices are to test on your actual data, measure quality separately from structure, test at production concurrency, and measure the tail not the mean.

I frame this as transparency, not moderation, since these images are history with legitimate places in the collection. The threshold is tuned to over-flag, because an unneeded content note costs little and a missed one costs much more. The flags do not restrict access or take anything down; they generate context.

cards.answer: I write that Mistral’s p99 latency jumps fivefold from concurrency 1 to 24, from 15 seconds to 74 seconds, with a sharp increase between c=4 and c=8. The cause is KV cache head-of-line blocking: Mistral’s 3,000 token prompts require large KV cache allocations, and at higher concurrency, the GPU VRAM can’t hold all in-flight KV states, leading to preemption and recomputation. At concurrency 24, Mistral’s p99 latency was 74 seconds compared to 39 seconds for Llama and 19 seconds for Qwen. This 74 second p99 meant roughly 1% of bill extractions blocked the processing queue for over a minute, and Mistral was eliminated because its chunk-size configuration was incompatible with the pipeline’s concurrency requirements.

cards.answer: Archives have always been a knowledge access problem bottlenecked on human time for description. The article shows that there has never been enough cataloguing capacity to keep up with the rate of acquisition, leaving material digitized but shelved with thin or no descriptions. I write that the description bottleneck is breaking, and that a multimodal model capable of describing an image in natural language is a cataloguing tool, not a moderation tool. cards.answer: Most failures come from one assumption: the model is smart enough to handle everything. It's not. Not yet. The systems that work handle preprocessing upfront, clean and structure data, provide schema-level context, design retrieval carefully, and use prompts that preserve context and coherence. Fix the system around the model and the model performs dramatically better.

agent or simple workflow
cards.answer: Agent territory: ambiguous decisions, logical reasoning, evolving inputs. The example I use is scraping trending topics in news. You can't hard-code what's trending, it changes constantly, and the model has to look at generalities and pick top themes. That's genuine agent work. Workflow automation: static process, consistent algorithm, consistent input and output. Same shape data coming in, same shape data going out. Don't use an agent for that. RPA: the simplest stuff, standard ETL, standard in and standard out. Old-school data science methods handle this perfectly. You don't need an AI agent. Rule of thumb: if the task requires the system to interpret something that isn't clearly defined, it's an agent. If it doesn't, it isn't, and forcing AI into it just adds complexity and cost.

cards.answer: Yes. I don't think agents are just an evolution of automation and APIs with better UX. They're a real shift in how work gets done. The part that's fundamentally different is ambiguity. Traditional pipelines follow deterministic logic, rule-based, conditional, predictable in. Agents operate where the decision isn't something you can hard-code. Where the model has to make a judgment call on fuzzy inputs. That's both the power and the risk. You're handing off the ambiguity to the AI, and whatever it decides is what happens next. If you think your role is safe, it probably isn't. Within the next 6 to 12 months, tasks, not whole jobs, but tasks, are going to start getting stripped out of roles at an accelerating pace. Whether that's a problem depends on your job. If it's mostly repetitive, yeah, be concerned. If it involves real decision-making, stakeholder work, strategy, and business impact, you're likely fine, but your job will evolve.

cards.answer: There has to be a way to anchor outputs back to truth. AI systems drift. The more they build on prior outputs, the worse it gets. So you need a base truth layer, validated data, known-good outputs, plus a way to detect drift and cross-check results. Some tolerance for variation is fine. Unlimited deviation isn't. My concrete example: in my legislation work, I have the Llama model generating category labels (new-school) and I also have an old-school clustering model generating categories from keywords (old-school). Both produce taxonomies. If one says Higher Education and the other says K-12 for the same bill, that's a flag. I can isolate the mismatches, inspect them, and figure out whether the model drifted or the data is weird. Hybrid validation like that is essential.

cards.answer: Everyone says 'AI augments humans' but most of the time that's vague or not really true. Both are happening simultaneously. The difference is what kind of work and how much oversight exists. Real augmentation: AI helps you move faster, you still own the outcome. You review, validate, correct, make the final call. AI accelerates, humans stay responsible for correctness. Where humans must stay in control right now: hiring, firing, legal outcomes, financial decisions, anything that directly affects someone's life. Those need multiple layers of review: the person who built the system approves how it works, stakeholders own the decisions, and someone audits continuously. Without that, it's not augmentation, it's uncontrolled automation in a trench coat.

cards.answer: When I was extracting 10+ structured features from legislation text, I originally thought asking each question separately would make parsing cleaner and more predictable. Turns out that's wrong. Bundling the questions in the same prompt gave better results because the model uses its earlier answers as context for later ones. If it already established 'this impacts higher education' and 'this affects students,' then when I later ask 'does this impact the university,' it answers yes coherently, and when I ask 'rate the impact as slight/moderate/very impactful,' it uses everything it just figured out. Context builds within the prompt. Isolating tasks too much loses coherence and reasoning continuity. Prompt engineering isn't just asking questions, it's designing the context the model reasons inside.

cards.answer: Short term, the weakest spot in the job market is entry-level. Companies don't need as many junior hires for basic tasks. AI tools let existing employees absorb that work. So instead of hiring a new grad, companies redistribute internally. But here's the contradiction: entry-level capability is actually higher than it's been in years. A fresh grad today can build faster, learn faster, and produce higher-quality work earlier than anyone four years ago. So my take is: if you need someone for straightforward work, just hire them. Don't overcomplicate hiring with unnecessary technical challenges. Every senior is using AI to write code. Every company has token quotas for productivity. cards.answer: In my legislation work, some bills were massive outliers, over 100,000 tokens, roughly 100x the size of a normal bill. Only about 5% of the data, but they added enormous noise. They were amendment-heavy bills, the same content updated over and over with every small change. Most of it added no context. What actually mattered was the latest changes, maybe the last thousand tokens. If you feed those directly into an AI system without preprocessing, it chunks them inefficiently, wastes compute, takes hours to process the worst-quality subset, and pollutes everything downstream. The fix wasn't an AI fix. It was a preprocessing fix. Detect the outliers, summarize them as 'amendment type, last changes attached,' and move on. Good data preprocessing should never be wasted AI logic.

What are the things you don't know? What are you losing because you didn't know them? That's the cost of not knowing, and it's where AI really earns its place. cards.answer: Even if the data is technically correct, if the model doesn't understand what the fields represent, it'll produce confident garbage. Poorly named columns, encoded values with no explanation, missing metadata, no documentation, all of it breaks the system quietly. You need a context layer: a data dictionary or 'data cookbook,' metadata descriptions, schema explanations embedded into prompts. It needs to know what each field represents, how fields relate, and what the data is actually capturing. Without that you're asking it to interpret something it doesn't understand, and it'll happily make something up.

cards.answer: Mountains over ocean, hands down. I live by the ocean and rarely go. I love being up high looking down on a lake, like Big Bear, and I'm looking forward to Asheville. Topanga Canyon is the best of both: a canyon in the mountains beside the ocean.

cards.answer: I sing everything badly and loudly. My karaoke song is "Sweet Child o' Mine." I also go for K-pop, 50 Cent and A Tribe Called Quest. cards.title: Places I love
questions: a place you love, or want to travel to?

where do you like to go
favorite beach
a place you love
where would you travel

does she like austin

cards.answer: My favorite place is anywhere with my family. Topanga Canyon is my go-to getaway and Tabletop in Solana Beach is my favorite San Diego beach. A lounge chair, a drink, and my family in the pool is my happy place. Austin, Texas felt like home, maybe even more than San Diego. Lately I love Raleigh, North Carolina, and I can see myself moving there.
